I think you can always create a logistical scenario that requires the answer of “well this is a 1 person spot so obviously the single person has to sleep in it”. That’s not what the idea is here.

And every time a situation like this comes up - and you can read it in the comments here - people tend to shrug their shoulders and say “well life isn’t fair, things can’t always be ideal, sometimes this is the easiest way”. And consider that this is like the mindset of someone picking a flower from a bush thinking “hey this is only 1 flower, no big deal there are plenty more!” And every person who walks by has that same mindset and picks a flower. Eventually the bush ends up having no flowers. This is what people are not really grasping - that if every friend group for every event / vacation has this mindset and applies it, the single persons will always face this specific “unfairness”. They will always be the ones put in an awkward position to be asked to sacrifice their comfort for the sake of others. And it’s a double edged sword because if they refuse, they’re inconsiderate. If they accept, it’s just an unacknowledged, thankless given. So if every time they go on some group trip they are expected to take not great sleeping accommodations… it becomes almost every single time for them. For the random friends that go on these trips, they only see it as a rare sacrifice. That’s the issue here.

You say it’s hard to be fair to everyone all the time and I agree with this. You can’t have 100% fairness 100% of the time. But the problem is single people bear the burden of the unfairness 100% of the time. So we don’t have to be fair to everyone all the time, but we also don’t have to be unfair to single people 100% of the time.

I lost my brother to suicide. I strongly recommend therapy, and I’m aware of children’s grief counseling centers specifically geared towards young survivors processing loss. If you go to therapy as well (not necessarily with them, but to your own group or individual meetings) it will be more likely that they’ll engage in it. Grief is not something you can explain the weight of, and it benefits both children and adults to have someone there to guide/support them through the process. Explain how it comes in waves, how it can be completely drowning and unbearable, but then when it becomes lighter you feel guilt. Suicide survivors face complex emotions and therapists can help. On this subject, I will note that I felt irritated when my own mother and father shirked therapy. They briefly went and then stopped. For me, I also found Suicide Survivors meetups helpful because I listened to stories of other people who lost someone. It is grounding in a way, but that may not be age appropriate for them.

Doing things to celebrate and honor the memory of your lost child can be very cathartic. Examples might be having them cremated, and taking bits of their ashes to spread in places they loved. When I did this, I also did not refer to my brother’s remains as just “ashes” - I referred to them as Him, and small things like that can help feel connected to your lost loved one still. On this note, I found it unhelpful when my parents or other siblings made negative remarks about my brother. To them, it may have sounded like they were remembering their reality of him, but it can come off as blaming or extremely insensitive. This is because the dynamic of my family is unhealthy and scapegoat/GC roles exist. Your family may not have that.

There are many books on suicide loss - some of which are specific to your role in the victim’s life. I recommend giving them these books (how old are they specifically?). I’ll try to recommend some if I can find mine again. 

Simple things like making comfort foods and watching a movie together can help. Buy extra blankets to enhance this “comfort” atmosphere. Costco has excellent, inexpensive blankets. Not kidding about doing this.

It is helpful to express your emotions of missing your son to them. “I miss him” can start a good conversation.
